title: [Chapitre] IX et IX bis. [Ateliers] : notes manuscrites (05-15/07/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: in the 1986 'Ateliers' notes Grothendieck axiomatizes combinatorial-topological 'multistructures' (cells or strata). A 'magicien' is a datum (M, ⊴, ≤°, |○|, F) together with an 'atelier' F of 'figures'. Here M is a set of structures; ≪, ≪̇ and ⊴ are face or refinement relations; X̃ is the set of structures attached to X (the faces of X, or its closure); |○| and || are incidence or meeting relations; F is a family of subsets of M called fragments or figures. Digression 3, dated 8 July, adds a 'compactology'.

(1) The extra structure is a subset M_c ⊂ M of 'compact' structures. In the left margin this datum is called a compactology, and the resulting object a 'magicien compactologiste'.

(2) Axiom Mag cpct 1 has two parts.
(a) If X ∈ M_c then X̃ is finite. Compact cells have finitely many faces.
(b) If X ∈ M_c and Y ≪ X then Y ∈ M_c. So M_c is downward closed, i.e. closed in the Alexandrov-type topology of the preorder (M, ≪). He asserts this is equivalent to closedness for ≪̇ and for ⊴.

(3) He announces two future axioms. Mag cpct 2 would be of Borel–Lebesgue (finite subcover) type. A second axiom would say that M_c is 'rich' in M, which subdivision should provide.

(4) He then states a compatibility axiom 'Mag et cpct' with the atelier F. If F ≪ X with F ∈ F and X ∈ M_c, then F̃ is finite. Better: for X ∈ M_c and every F ∈ F, the set {Y ∈ F̃ : Y || X, i.e. Y |○| X̃} is finite. In other words, every admissible figure is locally finite with respect to compact structures. This is the analogue of a locally finite family of cells (each compact set meets only finitely many cells), as in CW or polyhedral complexes.

(5) The margins define a figure F to be locally finite if, for every X ∈ M_c, #{Y ∈ F : Y |○| X} is finite. They also sketch 'compact figures', apparently finite sets of compact structures.

(6) The page ends with crossed-out attempts at the converse: given M_c, find the largest admissible F. The next page completes this. Locally finite parts form an 'antifiltre' (closed under subsets and finite unions). F_lf(M) is the largest atelier compatible with the compactology. Conversely, given F, the largest compatible compactology is M_c = {X : ∀F ∈ F, {Y ∈ F : X || Y} is finite}. This is a Galois correspondence between compactologies and ateliers via the 'meets finitely many' relation.

Purpose: to build into the axiomatic 'tame' combinatorial topology a notion of compactness and local finiteness. This would allow infinite but locally finite figures, e.g. non-compact polyhedra and stratified spaces with locally finite stratifications.
errors: The claim that closedness of M_c under ≪, ≪̇ and ⊴ are equivalent is asserted without proof. It holds only if these relations generate the same downward closure (e.g. ⊴ being the reflexive-transitive closure of ≪); this is not visible on the page.

The first version of the compatibility axiom (F ≪ X ⇒ F̃ finite) is replaced mid-sentence by the 'better' local-finiteness formulation. The page's prose here is syntactically broken by crossings-out; the clean statement only appears on the next page.
Mag cpct 2 and the 'richness' axiom are announced but not formulated.

ideas.what: Distinguished hereditary subset M_c of 'compact' cells with finitely many faces, closed downward under the face relation
ideas.modern_name: compactology / bornology on a poset of cells; finite subcomplexes of a CW or polyhedral complex
ideas.usually_credited_to: Compactologies in functional analysis: Waelbroeck, Buchwalter (1960s). Closure-finiteness: J.H.C. Whitehead (CW complexes, 1949).

ideas.what: Local finiteness of figures with respect to the compactology: each compact structure meets only finitely many members of a figure
ideas.modern_name: locally finite family / locally finite cell complex or stratification

ideas.what: Largest atelier compatible with a given compactology, and largest compactology compatible with a given atelier (Galois correspondence), completed on the next page
ideas.modern_name: Galois connection induced by the relation 'meets finitely many'; duality between bornologies and locally finite families
ideas.usually_credited_to: standard order-theoretic construction; no specific credit

ideas.what: Planned Borel–Lebesgue-type axiom and 'richness' of compacts via subdivision in an axiomatic tame topology
ideas.modern_name: axiomatic compactness in tame/o-minimal or combinatorial topology
ideas.usually_credited_to: tame topology program sketched in Esquisse d'un programme (1984); o-minimality (van den Dries, Pillay–Steinhorn, Knight)
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme discusses 'topologie modérée' in general terms only, not these axioms

missed.claim: Grothendieck plans, but never states on this page, a Borel–Lebesgue compactness axiom and a 'richness of compacts via subdivision' axiom for his combinatorial 'magiciens'. This is part of an unpublished axiomatic approach to tame topology through posets of strata with incidence relations, which has not been developed in the literature.
missed.quote: Par la suite, on sera amené sûrement à introduire un axiome Mag cpct 2, du type Borel-Lebesgue, et aussi que M_c est "riche" dans M (grâce aux subdivisions)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Purely combinatorial or poset-theoretic foundations for tame topology are of current interest (exit-path categories, stratified spaces, o-minimal triangulation). These notes show Grothendieck's intended treatment of non-compact, locally finite objects. The individual definitions on this page are standard, however.

missed.claim: The term 'compactologie' and the Galois duality between compactologies and locally finite families echo the Waelbroeck/Buchwalter bornology–compactology theory. Here that theory is transplanted into combinatorial stratified topology; the link between bornological ideas and tame stratified topology is not drawn in the literature.
missed.quote: Magiciens avec donnée de structures dites compactes (Magiciens compactologistes). Notion de figure localement finie.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a minor conceptual link. Bornological methods are used in analytic geometry (e.g. Clausen–Scholze, Ben-Bassat–Kremnizer) but not in combinatorial models of stratified spaces.

deep.surprise_reason: The page sets up routine definitions: a hereditary family of compact cells, local finiteness, and a compatibility axiom. These have standard analogues (closure-finite and locally finite complexes, bornologies). The interest lies only in its belonging to Grothendieck's unpublished 1986 axiomatic tame-topology framework and in the announced but unformulated compactness axioms.
transcription_corrections: The upper left margin likely reads 'Une donnée de M_c dans M s'appelle une compactologie' (cf. 'compactologie' on p.31), rather than only 'Une donnée de M_c dans M'.
'{+ceci : la topologie donnée, celle-ci,+}' should probably read 'une compactologie donnée' (consistent with the next page), not 'la topologie donnée'.

The fragment 'il existe un F fini dans Ỹ' mixes two lines. 'fini dans Ỹ' / 'i.e. Y |○| X̃ ... fini' belongs to the local-finiteness condition {Y ∈ F̃ : Y || X} finite. The separate crossed-out start reads 'Pour M_c donné, il existe un F ... le plus grand possible'.
The insertion '{+de M+}' after 'une partie M_c de M' is spurious; the superscript near 'On' is the margin text 'M'.

In the lower left margin, the definition is of a figure F ∈ F(M) being 'localement finie si ∀X ∈ M_c, #{Y ∈ F | Y |○| X} fini'; 'Figures compactes' appear to be defined via finiteness and membership in M_c.
